1.grade_fit_note: 'finally' with a dropped l is a grade 3-4 high-frequency word; the other sentences hold no competing hard word except 'probably'.
1.note: Key unambiguous. B and C use only common words, though B is padded ('with all of his friends') to match the others' length.

2.grade_fit_note: 'answer' (anwser) is a grade 3 word; the competing sentences have only 'studied' and 'straight' as anything to doubt.
2.note: Key unambiguous. C (rowed, boat, island, lake) gives a grade 5 student nothing to doubt.

3.grade_fit_note: Lowercase compass direction vs capitalized region is a standard grade 5-6 rule.
3.note: Clean 2x2 (South/south x Southwest/southwest). 'The Southwest' as a US region is capitalized in every major style guide.

4.grade_fit_note: 'beautiful' is a common grade 4-5 spelling word.
4.note: 2x2 over beu/beau and -ful/-full, so every misspelling shows up twice and frequency gives nothing away.

5.grade_fit_note: Proper adjectives from names and places, at grade 6.
5.note: Both Victorian and Persian are capitalized in mainstream dictionaries. Clean 2x2.

6.grade_fit_note: existence/existance is a classic grade 7-8 demon. The distractors harass, medieval and mischievous are well-chosen lures.
6.note: Good item: every distractor sentence holds a word students often misspell, so each could plausibly be flagged.

7.grade_fit_note: truly/truely is right for grades 5-6. column, measured and foreign compete.
7.note: Key unambiguous, and the distractors carry real lures (column, foreign).

8.grade_fit_note: privilege is a standard grade 7-8 demon word.
8.note: 2x2 over i/e and with/without d. No variant is accepted by any mainstream dictionary.

9.grade_fit_note: tomorrow is usually taught by grade 3-4.
9.note: 2x2 over m/mm and r/rr. The key is unambiguous.

10.grade_fit_note: Doubled consonants plus -ence makes this a strong grade 7-8 item.
10.note: 2x2 over c/cc and -ance/-ence. A student who knows 'occur' can still pick B.

11.note: 2x2 over m/mm and with/without e. The key is unambiguous.

12.note: 2x2 over c/cc and s/ss. The key is unambiguous.

13.grade_fit_note: committee is right for grade 7, and conscious, miniature and souvenir are good lures.
13.note: Strong distractor sentences, each with a hard but correctly spelled word.

14.note: 2x2 over the two unstressed vowels. The key is unambiguous.

15.grade_fit_note: especially, with the common 'expecially' error, fits grade 6.
15.note: 2x2 over es/ex and -ly/-lly. Both distractor features are real student errors.

16.grade_fit_note: Brand name vs following common noun is a grade 6 rule.
16.note: Intended key is C. These are invented brands, though, and real products often carry the generic word in the trademark (e.g. a product sold as 'Sunny Day Sunscreen'), so D, or the mixed options, can be argued. The stem never says what the brand names are.

17.note: 2x2 over hyp/hyph and -the-/-thi-. The 'hyph' distractors are a bit artificial but plausible.

18.grade_fit_note: Grade 5 students are typically taught that 'short words' stay lowercase. Knowing that 'Is' (a verb) is capitalized while 'the' is not is a grade 6-7 refinement.
18.note: APA, Chicago, MLA and AP all capitalize 'Is' and lowercase an internal 'the', so A is the only defensible key. B will draw most able grade 5 students.

19.grade_fit_note: embarrassed is a classic grade 7 demon.
19.note: 2x2 over r/rr and s/ss. The key is unambiguous.

20.grade_fit_note: A common noun reused after a proper name is a grade 5-6 rule.
20.note: Clean 2x2 over park/Park and river/River. Could be pitched slightly lower than 6.

21.grade_fit_note: guarantee is a grade 7-8 demon, and conscience, hygiene and possession are good lures.
21.note: Strong item. Every distractor sentence holds a frequently misspelled word.

22.grade_fit_note: disappear (prefix dis- plus appear) fits grades 4-5.
22.note: 2x2 over s/ss and p/pp. The key is unambiguous.

23.grade_fit_note: ir- plus -ible makes this a strong grade 8 item.
23.note: 2x2 over r/rr and -able/-ible. 'irresistable' is a common misspelling, not an accepted variant in mainstream dictionaries.

24.grade_fit_note: environment, with its silent n, is right for grade 6.
24.note: 2x2 over -ron-/-orn- and with/without the n. The key is unambiguous.

25.grade_fit_note: surveillance is at the hard end of grade 8.
25.note: 2x2 over l/ll and -ance/-ence. The key is unambiguous.

26.grade_fit_note: separate is a grade 5-6 demon, and capital (vs capitol), knowledge, business and February are good lures.
26.note: 'state capital' (the city) is correct, so A is a good capital/capitol lure.

27.note: 2x2 over c/cc and m/mm. The key is unambiguous.

28.grade_fit_note: A kinship term used as a name vs after a possessive is grade 4-5.
28.note: Clean 2x2 over Uncle/uncle and Grandmother/grandmother, with 'Grandpa' held constant as a name. The key is unambiguous.

29.grade_fit_note: cemetery is a grade 7 demon, and apparent, sincerely and valuable compete.
29.note: Good lures in A and B.

30.grade_fit_note: maintenance (not maintain + -ance) is a grade 8 demon.
30.note: 2x2 over the e/a in both unstressed syllables. The key is unambiguous.

31.grade_fit_note: A capitalized full-sentence quotation vs a lowercase fragment quotation is grade 6-7.
31.note: Clean 2x2. The integrated fragment quote ('called our passing "the best..."') takes lowercase in every mainstream style.

32.grade_fit_note: Historical documents and events fit grades 5-6.
32.note: Clean 2x2 over Rights/rights and Revolution/revolution. The key is unambiguous.

_batch.Spelling: There are two shapes. (1) The eight 'which sentence has a spelling error' items (1, 2, 6, 7, 13, 21, 26, 29) put the error at A once, C three times (6, 21, 26) and D four times (2, 7, 13, 29). It is never at B. Across a full form, a test-wise student can drop B, and D is the modal position. (Their distractor sentences also reuse the same small cast of names: Sam, Maya, Ben, Leo, Ana, Omar, Mia, Nora.) In the grade 5 items (1, 2), the error word is often the only non-trivial word in the set, so the error is found by elimination rather than spelling knowledge. The grade 7-8 items (6, 13, 21, 29) avoid this with hard but correct lure words. (2) All sixteen 'which word completes' items (4, 8-12, 14, 15, 17, 19, 22-25, 27, 30) are a strict 2x2 factorial: two binary features (single/double letter, vowel choice, suffix) crossed, so every feature value appears in exactly two options and no option is the consensus or 'middle'. Frequency and majority-feature strategies get nothing. Key letters are A x5, B x6, C x3, D x2, so the key is mildly front-loaded and D is under-used, though not enough to exploit on its own. Lengths do not mark the key. I found no wording or shape pattern that reveals the key in this group.
_batch.Capitalization: All eight items (3, 5, 16, 18, 20, 28, 31, 32) are a 2x2 factorial over two capitalization decisions in an otherwise identical sentence, so no option is the majority or 'between' choice. Keys are balanced (A: 18, 32; B: 5, 28; C: 16, 20; D: 3, 31), and the key cell varies: both capitalized (5, 32), both lowercase (16, 20, 28), mixed (3, 18, 31). So 'pick the most-capitalized' and 'pick the least-capitalized' each score only 2-3 of 8. The only recurring idea is 'a common noun is lowercase after the proper name it echoes' (20: park/river after Hollis River Park; 16: sunscreen/crackers after brands). That is the rule being tested, not a tell that works without knowing it. I found no position, length or wording tell.
